_note: Plain-language summaries of provisions. 'verification' = how far each entry has been checked: 'memory+secondary' means written from knowledge and cross-checked against secondary sources (orders, guides) but NOT yet against the bare act text on India Code. Re-check before relying on it.

entries.title: Projects must be registered with RERA
entries.summary: A promoter cannot advertise, market or sell flats in a real estate project without registering it with the state RERA. Projects that were ongoing when the Act started and had no completion certificate also had to register. Small projects (land up to 500 sq m or up to 8 apartments) are exempt.

entries.title: Extension of registration; meaning of force majeure
entries.summary: RERA can extend a project's registration in case of force majeure. The Act's explanation describes force majeure as war, flood, drought, fire, cyclone, earthquake or any other calamity caused by nature affecting the regular development of the project. Whether a builder's specific excuse (labour shortage, approvals, pandemic) counts is decided by the authority on facts.

entries.title: Builder is responsible for its promises until conveyance
entries.summary: The promoter is responsible for all obligations under the Act, the rules and the agreement for sale until the flat is conveyed to the buyer.

entries.title: No more than 10% advance without a registered agreement
entries.summary: A promoter cannot take more than 10% of the flat's cost as advance or application fee without first entering into a written agreement for sale and registering it.

entries.title: Delay in possession: refund or monthly interest
entries.summary: If the promoter fails to complete the flat or give possession by the date in the agreement for sale, the buyer can choose: (a) withdraw from the project and get back all money paid, with interest at the prescribed rate, plus compensation; or (b) stay in the project and get interest for every month of delay until possession is handed over.

entries.title: Buyer's right to refund with interest and compensation
entries.summary: The buyer is entitled to claim refund of amounts paid, with interest and compensation, if the promoter fails to comply with or is unable to give possession as per the agreement.

entries.title: Buyer must also pay on time
entries.summary: The buyer must make payments as per the agreement. If the buyer delays payments, the buyer can be made to pay interest at the prescribed rate. Builders often raise the buyer's own late payments as a defence, so keep proof of every payment.

entries.title: Who can file a complaint and where
entries.summary: Any aggrieved person can file a complaint with the state RERA authority or the adjudicating officer for any violation of the Act, rules or regulations by a promoter.

entries.title: Recovering money the builder is ordered to pay
entries.summary: If a promoter does not pay interest, penalty or compensation ordered under RERA, it can be recovered as arrears of land revenue.

entries.title: Builder must deposit before appealing
entries.summary: A promoter who appeals a RERA order to the Appellate Tribunal must first deposit at least 30% of the penalty, or the full amount payable to the buyer including interest and compensation, before the appeal is heard.

entries.title: Time limit to appeal
entries.summary: An appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order of the authority or adjudicating officer is to be filed within 60 days of receiving the order (the Tribunal can allow a late appeal for sufficient cause).

entries.title: Compensation is decided by the adjudicating officer
entries.summary: Claims for compensation are decided by an adjudicating officer appointed by the authority. Factors include the unfair gain made by the promoter, the loss caused to the buyer, and whether the default is repeated.

entries.title: Civil courts cannot hear RERA matters
entries.summary: Civil courts have no jurisdiction over matters that the RERA authority, adjudicating officer or Appellate Tribunal is empowered to decide.

entries.title: Other laws still apply
entries.summary: RERA is in addition to, not in place of, other laws. So a homebuyer may also have remedies under other laws such as consumer protection law, but should not run two parallel cases on the same claim without legal advice.

entries.act: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021
entries.title: Consumer commission as an alternative
entries.summary: A homebuyer can approach a consumer commission for deficiency in service. Which commission depends on the amount paid as consideration: District Commission up to Rs 50 lakh, State Commission above Rs 50 lakh up to Rs 2 crore, National Commission above Rs 2 crore.
entries.source: Consumer Protection Act 2019; Jurisdiction Rules 2021 — India Code / consumeraffairs.nic.in

entries.title: Two-year limit for consumer complaints
entries.summary: A consumer complaint should be filed within two years from when the cause of action arose; delay can be condoned for sufficient cause. In a continuing delay of possession the cause of action may be treated as continuing, but this depends on facts.
entries.source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, s.69 — India Code (indiacode.nic.in)

entries.title: Free legal aid
entries.summary: Certain people are entitled to free legal services, including women, children, members of SC/ST, persons with disabilities, industrial workmen, people in custody, disaster victims, and people below a state-notified income limit. Apply at the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) or call the NALSA helpline 15100.
entries.source: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987, s.12 — nalsa.gov.in
